steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on ensembles of quantum classifiers. Cover the NISQ limitations that motivate ensembles, related work on quantum ensemble methods, what our hybrid scheme uses and how we evaluate it, and end with the structure of the article.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- QML and the NISQ era: why circuits must be small
- Ensemble methods and why they help on NISQ devices
- Related work: quantum ensemble methods
- This work: hybrid scheme, methods, QRAM caveat, evaluation and results
- Article structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
QML and NISQ
- QML: quantum algorithms for ML problems, more efficient than classical counterparts
- enough fully connected qubits -> quantum advantage vs. classical supercomputers on various tasks, practical problems
- current era: Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ); noisy devices, limited qubits
- gate-based devices: noise impact grows with circuit depth and size
- encoding large data challenging; results affected by noise
- circuits must be smaller to run on current architectures -> progress on real-world challenges despite limits

Ensembles
- combine predictions of multiple models
- goal: better prediction accuracy and stability via model diversity
- classical ensembles reduce computational requirements in quantum computation
- internal models compact (smaller training subsets)
- ensembles let quantum algorithms run on NISQ devices: more efficient resource usage than single larger models (smaller circuits)

Quantum ensemble methods (related work)
- Schuld and Petruccione; Abbas et al.: quantum ensemble classifiers based on Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA); non-trainable classifiers, assumption large ensemble of weak classifiers performs well
- Araujo and da Silva: quantum ensemble of trainable classifiers; superposition of quantum classifiers = quantum neural networks
- Macalauso et al.: quantum ensemble framework based on bagging; exponential growth of ensemble size, linear increase in circuit depth
- Windridge and Nagarajan: quantum-SVM-based attribute bootstrap aggregation; superposition of quantum decision hyperplanes for attribute selection
- Qin et al.; Zhang and Wang: hybrid techniques combining quantum classification algorithms; parallel combination of variational quantum classifiers can beat SOTA

This work
- implementation + empirical evaluation of ensembles of quantum classifiers
- hybrid: classical ensemble methods + quantum classification algorithms
- ensembles: bootstrap, boosting, stacking
- quantum classifiers: quantum cosine classifier, quantum distance classifier, quantum k -nearest neighbors (quantum k -NN)
- need quantum random access memory (QRAM) for speedup; no working QRAM prototypes yet
- focus: empirical accuracy, not quantum time advantage
- binary classification on real-world datasets
- results: accuracy advantage over single classifiers, more robustness; mitigates unsuitable data normalizations and repeated measurement inaccuracies

Structure
- Section 2 background; Section 3 hybrid scheme + implementation; Section 4 experiments + results; Section 5 conclusion

If enough fully connected qubits were available, a quantum advantage (compared to classical supercomputers) could be reached on different tasks, and practical problems could be tackled effectively. But the current era, which is called Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ), has noisy devices with limited numbers of qubits. Also, in gate-based quantum devices the impact of noise gets bigger as the depth and size of the circuit grow. So encoding large amounts of data is challenging, and noise affects the quality of the results a lot. The size of the circuits must be reduced to run quantum algorithms on the current architectures. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Quantum machine learning (QML) is a recent field of research that aims to develop quantum algorithms that solve machine learning problems more efficiently than the classical counterparts. If enough fully connected qubits were available, a quantum advantage (compared to classical supercomputers) could be reached on different tasks, and practical problems could be tackled effectively. But the current era, which is called Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ), has noisy devices with limited numbers of qubits. Also, in gate-based quantum devices the impact of noise gets bigger as the depth and size of the circuit grow. So encoding large amounts of data is challenging, and noise affects the quality of the results a lot. The size of the circuits must be reduced to run quantum algorithms on the current architectures. This way, even with the current limitations, practical problems could be addressed, and there can be progress towards solving real-world challenges with quantum computing technologies.

Ensemble methods are a machine learning technique that is widely used, and they combine the predictions of multiple models. The idea is to improve prediction accuracy and stability by exploiting the diversity of the models. In quantum computation, classical ensembles are an effective way to reduce computational requirements, because the internal models usually have compact sizes since they are trained on smaller subsets of the data. In practice, ensemble methods make it possible to run quantum algorithms on NISQ devices, since they use resources more efficiently than single larger models (the quantum circuits are smaller).

Quantum ensemble methods have also been developed. For example, Schuld and Petruccione and Abbas et al. have proposed quantum ensemble classifiers based on Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA). These ensembles use non-trainable classifiers, and they assume that a large ensemble of weak classifiers can get good performance. Araujo and da Silva instead presented a quantum ensemble of trainable classifiers. They considered a superposition of quantum classifiers, where the classifiers are quantum neural networks. Macalauso et al. proposed a quantum ensemble framework that is based on bagging and where the ensemble size grows exponentially while the circuit depth only increases linearly. Windridge and Nagarajan present a quantum-SVM-based attribute bootstrap aggregation, where a superposition of quantum decision hyperplanes is used to do attribute selection. Finally, Qin et al. and Zhang and Wang proposed hybrid techniques to combine quantum classification algorithms efficiently, and they showed that combining multiple variational quantum classifiers in parallel can do better than state-of-the-art classification methods.

In this work we present an implementation of ensembles of quantum classifiers and an empirical evaluation of them. The scheme we propose is hybrid, with classical ensemble methods and quantum classification algorithms. For the ensemble methods we consider bootstrap, boosting, and stacking. For the quantum classifiers we consider a quantum cosine classifier, a quantum distance classifier, and a quantum k -nearest neighbors (quantum k -NN) classifier. Like many other quantum machine learning algorithms, the quantum algorithms used here need a quantum random access memory (QRAM) to get a speedup compared to classical computation. Working prototypes of QRAMs do not exist yet. But this work does not focus on the possible quantum time advantage, it focuses on the empirical evaluation of the scheme in terms of accuracy. For this, the methods were evaluated on a binary classification task on real-world datasets. The results showed an accuracy advantage compared to single classifiers and also better robustness. The ensembles were able to mitigate both unsuitable data normalizations and repeated measurement inaccuracies.

The article is structured as follows. Section 2 gives some background information. Section 3 introduces the hybrid scheme and the implementation details. Section 4 is about the experiments and the results. Section 5 concludes the work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Quantum machine learning (QML) is a recent field of research that aims at developing quantum algorithms for solving machine learning problems more efficiently than their classical counterparts [1]. If a sufficient number of fully connected qubits were available, a quantum advantage (with respect to classical supercomputers) could be achieved on different tasks and practical problems could be tackled effectively. However, the current era, known as Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) [2], is characterised by noisy devices with limited numbers of qubits. Additionally, in gate-based quantum devices, the impact of noise increases with the circuit's depth and size. As a consequence, encoding large amounts of data is challenging, and the quality of the results is significantly affected by noise. To execute quantum algorithms on current architectures, the size of the circuits must be reduced. In this way, despite the current limitations, practical problems could be addressed, making progress towards solving real-world challenges with quantum computing technologies.

Ensemble methods are a widely used machine learning technique that combines the predictions of multiple models [3]. This approach aims at enhancing prediction accuracy and stability by exploiting model diversity. In the context of quantum computation, classical ensembles are an effective way to reduce computational requirements, since the internal models typically have compact sizes due to the smaller data subsets used for training. In practice, ensemble methods allow quantum algorithms to be executed on NISQ devices thanks to more efficient resource usage with respect to single larger models (the quantum circuits involved are smaller).

Quantum ensemble methods have also been developed. For instance, Schuld and Petruccione [4] and Abbas et al. [5] have proposed quantum ensemble classifiers based on Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA). These ensembles exploit non-trainable classifiers, under the assumption that a large ensemble of weak classifiers can achieve good performance. Instead, Araujo and da Silva have presented a quantum ensemble of trainable classifiers [6], considering a superposition of quantum classifiers in which the classifiers are quantum neural networks. Macalauso et al. have proposed a quantum ensemble framework [7] based on bagging, characterised by an exponential growth of the ensemble size at the price of a linear increase in circuit depth. Windridge and Nagarajan [8] present a quantum-SVM-based attribute bootstrap aggregation, in which a superposition of quantum decision hyperplanes is used to perform attribute selection. Finally, Qin et al. [9] and Zhang and Wang [10] have proposed hybrid techniques to efficiently combine quantum classification algorithms, showing that the parallel combination of multiple variational quantum classifiers can outperform state-of-the-art classification methods.

In this work, we present an implementation and empirical evaluation of ensembles of quantum classifiers. The proposed scheme is hybrid, combining classical ensemble methods and quantum classification algorithms. As ensemble methods, bootstrap [11], boosting [12], and stacking [13] have been taken into account. As quantum classifiers, a quantum cosine classifier [14], a quantum distance classifier [15], and a quantum k -nearest neighbors (quantum k -NN) classifier [16,17] have been considered. Like many other quantum machine learning algorithms, the quantum algorithms employed here require a quantum random access memory (QRAM) [18] to achieve a speedup with respect to classical computation, and working prototypes of QRAMs have not been developed yet. However, this work does not focus on the potential quantum time advantage but on the empirical evaluation of the scheme in terms of accuracy. To this end, the methods have been evaluated on a binary classification task on real-world datasets. The results show an accuracy advantage with respect to single classifiers as well as improved robustness: the ensembles were able to mitigate both unsuitable data normalizations and repeated measurement inaccuracies.

The article is structured as follows: Section 2 provides background information; Section 3 introduces the hybrid scheme and the implementation details; Section 4 deals with the experiments performed and the results obtained; Section 5 concludes the work.
